trace.topic: Dear SaaStr: Our CFO Sounds Very Polished but We are Missing the Burn Rate Plan Almost Every Month. What Should I Do?
trace.goal: Give direct founder advice on diagnosing and handling a finance execution gap.
expected_facts: The answer should separate polish from operational competence.
It should explain that missing burn planning repeatedly is a serious execution issue, not a communication issue.
It should recommend concrete corrective actions such as tighter forecasting, direct review, or leadership change if the gap persists.
rubric_must_haves: States clearly that recurring miss on burn planning is a real risk.
Offers practical next steps for the founder.
Uses a direct operator tone rather than HR-speak.
Explains when coaching is enough and when replacement may be necessary.
trace.gold_reference: A strong answer should say that sounding polished does not matter if the finance leader keeps missing the burn plan. Founders need accurate forecasting, tight cash discipline, and fast escalation when trust in the numbers breaks. The right move is to inspect the process directly, tighten controls, and decide quickly whether this is a fixable systems problem or a leadership problem.

trace.answer: Dear SaaStr: My VPS is very polished but we miss our monthly burn plan almost every month. How do I get them to hit the mark? A few thoughts here: First, ask if they have a real dashboard. Most don’t. It’s too much work. Ask what their top 3 metrics are to manage the company. This usually gets a pause. They’ll say revenue, churn, etc. But then they won’t know exactly how many leads they need this quarter to achieve those goals. Or any KPIs tied to hiring. You want to see all these tied together in one place. Second, ask when was the last time they built a model themselves? If never — again, most aren't up for the task — you need someone else. Not necessarily a great VP of Finance or CFO. Just someone who knows enough finance to build a model (and understand cash flow) … that does it regularly. And third, realize there are only so many dollars in the bank. There just are. So set aside half a day once a month to go over it together and figure out why we missed our goal. And then make adjustments going forward. Because you can always grow faster than planned. But you can’t spend more than you have. That’s the thing.

retrieval_hits.text: 10 Simple Ideas to Help Manage the Burn So, for many of us in SaaS, these are still some of the better of times. The Cloud is bigger than ever, CIOs are buying more than ever, and SaaS is still on a roll, no matter how it may feel at times. But public stock prices are still way down, and venture capital is much tighter than it was outside of AI Mania. So many of you will want to manage the burn more carefully. But you can’t cut your way to growth. So what should a CEO do? A few simple thoughts: #1. Let go of your bottom 10%-15% of sales reps, concentrate leads in the best reps. This always gives you both a top-line boost (the top reps close more per lead), and gives you room to hire more reps at the same budget. #2. Have a firm, management-team wide burn rate budget. And stick to it. Pick a fixed amount of cash you can burn each month, period. And make all your VPs accountable to it. They can negotiate themselves on where to spend incremental revenue and dollars. #3. Just move on from any VP that isn’t getting it done They almost always overspend compared to the VPs that overperform. They hire mediocre folks on their team. And they overspend to try to make their plan. #4. Spend more time with existing customers. And go save the ones on the fence I know this is a broken record on SaaStr, but it works. Relatively speaking, the easiest sales are from your existing customers. So go spend more time with them. And go save the ones on the fence. #5. Build an L4M Model, and update it every month. Religiously.

4. Set a burn-rate budget for each and every month
.
This will focus your team and de-stress your life.  Most of us come up with a rough budget for the year, but not a
burn-rate budget
for
each month
.  This will force everyone on the team, starting Monday, to collaborate on hiring and other trade-offs.  If you go over the budget, now everyone will know.  In close to real time.  This will almost immediately improve the efficiency of your limited budgets, and improve teamwork.  And you will make better decisions on where to deploy your limited resources.  Which will not just manage your burn rate — but increase your revenues.  Starting Monday.  More
here
.

Burn Rate & Runway
: This is the scary one, but the most important. The green line is your cash balance. The red line is your cumulative burn. Where they intersect? That’s your Zero Cash Date. In this example, the company has burned $27.4M cumulatively and is trending toward a crossover point around September 2026. That’s about 10 months of runway. Not great. Needs immediate attention. The 3 Financial Plans You Need for The Year:  C-90, C-60 and C-10 (Updated)
Why This Changes Everything
Once you have your C60 plan — your actual, realistic base case — you can do three critical things:

1. Build your hiring plan.
You know exactly how much revenue you’ll likely generate, so you can model out how many reps, engineers, or support staff you can actually afford to hire. No more “let’s hire 5 people and hope it works out.”

4. Set a burn-rate budget for each and every month.
This will focus your team and de-stress your life.  Most of us come up with a rough budget for the year, but not a burn-rate budget for
each month
.  This will force everyone on the team, starting Monday, to collaborate on hiring and other trade-offs.  If you go over the budget, now everyone will know. In close to real-time.  This will almost immediately improve the efficiency of your limited budgets, and improve teamwork.  And you will make better decisions on where to deploy your limited resources.  Which will not just manage your burn rate — but increase your revenues.  Starting Monday.
